utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, Vladimir Santic, also known as "Vlado."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. We have learned this morning that Witness No. 13 on the list will not be able to come this morning for health reasons. The Victims and Witnesses Unit has just told us about this, and yesterday evening, I met myself this witness, who told me that he had some difficulty adapting to The Hague. Indeed, he has flown from Bosnia, it is the first time he has taken a plane, so he feels a bit ill and he won't be able to come this morning. As for the two other witnesses, the first to come to testify before you will be No. 12 and then No. 11 will come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Well, these are the facts of life. There's nothing we can do about it. All right then. So this witness who is now feeling ill, will we see him Monday morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I do hope so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So do we.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I would now call Witness U. In relation to protection measures, Your Honours, this witness has asked for face protection and name protection. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honours, in terms of procedure, I would ask that the majority of the session be in open session but the final part of the session being closed where some more identifying details will be necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So we are now in open session, I gather.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness U.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, above the Z, the diacritical mark is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honours, to assist the Court in putting this witness's evidence in context, I ask that Your Honours refer to Exhibit 208, which is a list, and on the first portion of that list, page number 13. This witness was living in the house of the person given the identification number 399. That's the second column. Later in his evidence, he will point that house out to the Court, but so that Your Honours can understand the evidence more easily ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness U, I'd like to advise you that the Court has given you protection measures, protection in relation to your face - your face will be disguised on public TV - and also in relation to your name. I will refer to you as Witness U. In relation to specific detail that we may ask for in relation to other people you saw on this day, we will ask for those details more at the end of the testimony when that will be in closed session. We will advise you at that time, but until then, if you can be more general in describing people rather than in particular in the beginning. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness U, on the 16th of April, 1993, you lived in the village of Ahmici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court where you originally came from in 1992 before you arrived in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: I came from Karaula.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You lived there most of your life?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes, I lived in Karaula all my life. I was an inhabitant of Karaula.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In November '92, did you have to leave Karaula?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: We had to leave Karaula under the pressure of the Serb or Chetnik aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you move to another village before you arrived at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: We first came to the village of Dubravica where we were put up, my family was put up; then we were accommodated in a neighbouring village near Ahmici, and then we had to leave that village also; and then we went to the village of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About what time did you arrive at the neighbouring village to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: It was approximately February. I cannot recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Without mentioning the name of the village, can you describe to the Court the types of people that populated the village, their ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: This village, in terms of the ethnic origin of the people, was mostly populated by Croatian people, by Catholics, there was a fewer number of Muslims living in the village, and the other part, the vacationing cottages, I don't know how that was populated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many Muslim families were living in the village when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Down there where I lived in that village, there was some six or seven families living in the lower section, and those were Muslim families, and the rest of the families were all Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you say "Catholic," are you referring to Bosnian Croat, Bosnian Serb, Bosnian Muslim? Which?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: I'm referring to Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Serbs, and Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how long did you stay in the village before moving to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: I stayed there for about a month and a half, about 45 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Why was it that you moved to the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: The pressures being brought to bear by the Bosnian Croats. They seized property, they maltreated, they searched the houses looking for weapons, so it was not a place to live in, to survive, for the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was your house searched?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: On about how many occasions was your house searched?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: During my stay, my house was searched three times as were all of the houses of the Muslims, but I can't tell you exactly how many times the others were searched.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who, in fact, searched the houses? Did they belong to any military group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: A military formation bearing the insignia of the HVO, the military police of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you know any of the people that searched your houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: I did. I didn't know them from before, but I knew them at that moment. The gentlemen nicknamed Cicko and Rutko, as the locals called them, but I personally did not know them because I had never been in that village before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how old were Cicko and Rutko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Between 25 and 30 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What were they searching your house for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: For a while, I was a metal worker, and every time when I came, they came to search for weapons, searching my house, checking to see whether I had been preparing myself when I, in no case, was in possession of any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that there was stealing occurring in the village. Stealing was occurring in relation to who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who was stealing what from who? Who had things stolen from them in the village? Which ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: The gentleman who came as a refugee from Jajce, Vasid. From him, they seized his car. Then from another refugee, Ganic Nahid, they also confiscated his car and some other property and searched the house and they maltreated the family. So that under such pressures, all of us, the rest of the Muslim population of the village, left and went to the village of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you say they were stealing from these people you have just mentioned, who is "they"? What military group did they belong to, if any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: I do not know whether they belonged to a military formation, but they -- with insignia and camouflage uniforms, there were lads, there were young men, I already said who they were, and those very same persons, on another occasion, maltreated my minor son looking for some weapons, having him take his clothes off in order to find something, to exert pressure, but as they couldn't find anything, the only thing they did was subject him to fear, but they could not find anything. After all this had been done, I myself felt, as did all the others, that we were not welcome in that place, and we searched for another location, another place. Another thing happened, which was a murder, a killing in that village. It was also a Bosniak Muslim, and after we had gone through all that, we saw that we were not suitable, and we left that place and went to seek refuge in another place, namely the village of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you witness that killing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: No, I did not. I only heard an explosion. I was present at the funeral, but I did not witness the killing because it happened late at night and I was not a witness to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court briefly how that killing occurred from what you heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: According to what I had heard from my neighbours, there was no quarrel or grudge between those two persons involved. The only reason for that was that he was a member of the army, and at night his house was blown up and he was killed, and I cannot tell you what the actual reasons were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Which army was he a member of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: B and H.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness U, do you know of a location near that village called the Bungalow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Between these two villages, there is a location, a site, a hotel or a bungalow, yes, I know it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court, at the time that you were staying at that village, what the Bungalow was and what it was used for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: As we were coming to that village, we could see that the bungalows were used for some sort of a military facility because there was some heavy weaponry, a part of heavy weaponry was there, and the insignias were worn on camouflage uniforms and on black uniforms which one could see every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Which military group did the Bungalow relate to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: The military formations of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You have said that because of these happenings towards Muslims, you and some other families left and went to Ahmici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How was it that you decided to go to Ahmici? Was there an offer of housing there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: At that moment, nobody offered us any accommodation initially and we sought protection there because the population there is Muslim, so we tried to find accommodation in the summer vacationing cottages and some in the houses proper, in the real houses, and so we were helped by the neighbours there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many families from this village went to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Just a minute. I have to think of the exact number. Three families, refugee families, that fled came to the village of Ahmici, and other families were put up by other families in Vrhovine, around Vitez and so on, but the number of families which left the village was six or seven and only one family remained, a family of an intermarried couple. They are the only ones who remained in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You finally found a house in Ahmici to stay at, without mentioning the name of the house at this stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You have said this before, but can you remind us the exact time that you arrived in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact date. It was the month of February. I'm not quite sure. I cannot say what the exact date was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You arrived in Ahmici with your family; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your wife and children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes, my wife and children and a sister of mine was with us. My sister, my two children, and my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you arrived at Ahmici, or shortly after, there were some meetings that were held in the Ahmici village. Can you tell the Court what those meetings were about that you attended?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Before I came to the village of Ahmici from that village, we'd meet in connection with the complaints of the Muslims, the Bosniak Muslims, against things being done by the Croats, so we went to seek refuge and see to the restoration of order that was promised, that that would indeed be so, but words were one thing and actions were quite a different matter. We talked about trust, confidence between the Bosniak Muslims and the Bosnian Croats, that they would not harm one another, that there should be no fears, that there should be no suspicions, but after a while, what happened happened, and it happened in the village of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: These meetings, were they in relation to the refugees, namely yourself, coming from that other village, and the problems that occurred in that other village, or were the meetings in relation to possible problems that may have been occurring in Ahmici village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Not knowing what the situation was like in the village of Ahmici, we came up there to seek accommodation from the village from which we came, in the village of Ahmici. And people were asking that someone guarantee us our life in that village, but there was no one who could do such a thing. No one could guarantee that to us. So at this meeting -- at this meeting we discussed the question of the refugees, of the people who had fled, whom I represented, and the locals. They were discussing the issue of their own stability of their own security and the security of both them and us, and we came there as a third party to ask for our own security to also be a consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was it ever suggested that you go back to the village that you've just come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes, it was suggested that we go back. We sought guarantees in that village, which we could not get, so we stayed. We could not return.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who did you seek those guarantees from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: From the Croatian people and the Civil Defence with which we registered, to whom we applied when we came to that village, from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why couldn't these people guarantee that protection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: The answer which was given to us is that things were being done by extremists, that it was not them. That they couldn't guarantee on behalf of them anything, the extremists.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And which extremists were they referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: They had in mind the Croatian people, extremists, who were searching the houses, maltreating the people, looting. And those extremists wore the insignia of the HVO, under the command of which they were. And I know that for a fact that they wore such insignia. And who was in command? That is one thing do I not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So Croats from this village, having been unable to guarantee your security back in that village, you decided to stay in the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: No, they were not. We decided to stay in the village of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were you involved in any humanitarian aid tasks whilst you were in the village of Ahmici, and if not before that as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes, I was. In my spare time I -- I engaged in the distribution of humanitarian relief supplies and food to refugees in that village, and after the return there was more refugees, so that I distributed relief aid to all of them in the village of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to give a figure to the Court about how many -- about how many refugees you gave aid to in the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: I cannot say what the exact number of families was. The number changed, but it was sometimes up to 150 people, sometimes more and sometimes less, who were on the list for receiving humanitarian aid. And the families sometimes united when they sought and found accommodation, so that I cannot say what the exact number of families was. They came from all parts, from Karaula and other places from which people fled in order to seek refugee in the village of Ahmici, and to be put up with someone and to find protection for themselves and for their lives there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to say what ethnic group these refugees belonged to, if they belonged to one -- one group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: During my stay there, all the refugees were Bosnian Muslims, during my stay in the village of Ahmici, because -- and whether there were any others before or after, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how many times did you deliver aid to the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Well, I was only in charge of transporting from the Merhamet Society, which was distributing, doing the distributing. And I did that about once a month, sometimes more, depending on when -- what particular supplies arrived and could be distributed, because it involved clothing and food, and they did not all arrive at the same time. So one day we would be distributing the flour, another day the sugar, on a third day yet blankets. I cannot tell you exactly what the number of times was, but we had one lot a month which was distributed to the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was there one distribution point in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes, there was one point. It was usually done at the school, at a certain point, a certain hour, and the people would get whatever was their allotted portion depending on the -- their numbers. And it would be distributed in equal parts -- into equal parts to all the people in need in the village of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And apart from that was the school used as a school or was it used as something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: The school was only used as a school and for these distributions of humanitarian relief supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And before the 16th of April, how long had you been living in the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Before the 16th of April, I had been there for a month or a month and a half. Since -- from February to April. I cannot tell you the exact date when I moved from that previous village to this village. It was February, that I'm sure of. Perhaps mid-February. So I had been there for about 60 days before that, in the village of Ahmici that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If you can go back to the day before the 16th of April, was there anything significant that happened to you as you delivered humanitarian aid to the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: I didn't catch the question, I'm sorry. Well, as every day doing my duty, I had a horse and cart, I went to fetch -- to get the humanitarian aid. I could go freely, there were no searches, no controls. Everything seemed to be quite in order, provided that -- however, that particular morning, the worst, the most tragic and most abominable things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That -- this morning is now what I would like to concentrate on. Can you tell the Court, on the 16th of April, in the morning, about what time did you hear something unusual?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: I don't know the exact time, because these were instances of the greatest excitement. It was the time of prayer of the Bosnian Muslims, and all of a sudden a strong blast could be heard, a strong explosion which echoed so that I got up -- I sprang up to see what was happening around me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you look out a window?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I got up, I looked out the window. Shooting could be heard. I didn't know from where it was coming. It was coming from all quarters, from all sides. Four lads, soldiers, armed, above my village -- or, rather, above my house from the neighbouring village were nearing us from up there. They passed by my house towards a wood, through a wood, which stretches to the store, to the shop, the Sutre, wearing insignia and the white ribbon on their heads. I was not aware -- I didn't know what was happening at that moment. I couldn't see what was happening. I could only see these lads, these men, these soldiers with HVO insignia. I waited. I waited to see whether somebody would come to inform me -- tell me something, but everybody was looking after themselves. People who knew what was happening, they went out, and if they saw somebody else they would also tell them to go. So at that moment, not perhaps right away, perhaps the shooting had died down a bit, I also set out to go, to leave that house, that house which was mine at that moment, for I could see that the other people were also anxious to leave the houses, the villagers, the locals in the village, so I also saw that I had to go too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you said that you saw the locals were leaving the village or wanted to leave, or knew that the locals wanted to leave the village, what did you, in fact, see? Which direction did you see them leaving the village or attempting to leave the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: I was in a house which was just by the road. Women and children were there. They were crying, they were restless. They were leaving their homes, their villages from the directions where they all were. They all wanted to get to Gornji Ahmici, above the village, to get to the free territory, if it was free. Some people managed to reach it, others stayed there forever, killed, expelled, whatever. Weapons were used against them too. Most of these people were women and children. There weren't any grown-up people there, grown-up men, at least not while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just to give the Court a bit more of an understanding of where you were, without referring to a map at the moment, you were -- the house you were staying at, that was along side of the road; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And that road led up to the Sutre store; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the Sutre store is a place that you had visited earlier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I got supplies there, whatever I needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that when you heard the gunfire, you looked out the window and you saw some HVO soldiers. Which direction -- you said they were headed -- sorry. You said they were heading toward the Sutre store; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You also referred to women and children trying to leave the village. Was that what you first saw or did that happen shortly afterwards, after you heard the gunfire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: No. This was happening after the shooting. Nothing was happening before the shooting. It is the early morning, between day and night. Everything happened after the shooting that took place at day-break on the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Which direction were the women and children heading towards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: The women and children were walking towards the shop, towards the Sutre shop, through the valley, along the road. I don't know. I saw the people who were passing by my house, and I did not get to see those who were passing on the other side. I wasn't there, so I can't tell you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what did you decide to do once you saw all of this going on? What did you and your family decide to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: When I saw everybody leaving, going away, I saw that there was pressure from the military that was on. I realised that I could not defend myself. So what was left to me? (redacted) (redacted) I took her into my arms, and I told the rest of my family members, "Follow me and let us get out of this hell, this terrible thing that has been taking place over here." As we set out, I went out of the house first, then the members of my family followed, two children, my wife that is, my brother and my sister-in-law who were there, they were visiting, and then the other locals joined us. There was a bit of quiet as we were leaving towards the Sutre shop. Panic still prevailed though. Houses were burning, and they were torched. Shooting could be heard. We are trying to protect ourselves and to find the best way to go, the safest way to go. We crossed the main road, we came to a hill -- or rather, two hills. We couldn't pass there. We were stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And -- sorry, go on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: We were stopped there. We thought that those were soldiers or that they were civilians, and then we heard shooting again. We sat down so that they couldn't notice us that easily. There were some women who were killed there and others were wounded. At that moment Nadira was wounded, who stood in front of me -- or, rather, sat in front of me, or squatted in front of me. She was hit in the head. I see that there was no way for me to go. I wasn't familiar with the place. I hadn't lived there for a long time. I went back again, because I realised that I could not go ahead. As I was going back, I was wounded in my left arm, in the back of my left arm. My sister, whom I was holding in my arms, was wounded a little bit. It was just her sweatshirt that was cut a bit, but her body was really defended by this so it was just scarred a little bit. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: I was there with my family, went back again taking the same route, going back to the same house. A local woman, Smaila came back. (redacted) (redacted), and we awaited our fate, to see what our fate would be, whether we could go ahead or whether the whole situation would calm down. However, it did not. We waited for a certain period of time. We didn't know where to go. A woman came, a refugee. Her young son was killed, as well as her husband, and she told us that we should hide, because they were killing all males, all males indiscriminately. And she said, "Hide even in a mouse hole, but just hide." And I knew there was a storage space, a pantry, in the garage. My brother, my son and I walked into the garage, and we hid in that pit, and we were waiting to see what would happen next and what our fate would be. After a short while, I don't really know for how long this went on, I didn't have a wristwatch or anything, two soldiers came. They were shooting bursts of gunfire at the door and they were shouting, "Get out." There was no one to get out. There were only civilians, women, children. So it was under this pressure that they got out. I cannot say that anyone was dragging them or something, but they did hold their rifles though and they said, "Get out. Move on further." And I stayed hidden in this pit. And then I went back to the house, and no one found me for four or five days. And I didn't know which way to go, where to go, who I should surrender myself to, what I should do with myself. There were people who were collecting corpses though, and that is when we decided to surrender ourselves to them, and that is when we revealed ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Just to provide the Court a little more detail about what happened when you were shot; the group that you were with just before you were shot, about how big was that, the numbers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: As far as I know, this group consisted of some 15 to 20 civilians who were there at that point in time when we stopped there too. About 20 civilians really.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how many of them were women and children, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: I was there, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: (redacted)who was perhaps three or four years old at that time

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: (redacted)Most of them were women and children. It was only us, the refugees, who were men,(redacted) (redacted) All rest were women,

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: (redacted)but I didn't know people whom I wasn't very close to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that you tried to leave the village with these people and you headed up towards the Sutre store along the road and then you said you got to the main road; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: When I got to the main road, I crossed it, and then I tried to reach the main road too, but I didn't manage to do that as we were wounded, so then we had to go back. We did cross the road, but we didn't manage to continue along the road leading out of Donja Ahmici and into Gornji Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, if it's possible, which direction the shooting was coming from, from which you were shot and the others in the group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: In my view, I stood at some point before the Sutre shop and it was coming from up there. I saw soldiers there too. And shooting was coming from other sides, but I couldn't see the rest. I could hear it, though, but as I was standing there at that point, I could see the soldiers myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how far away were the soldiers to the Sutre shop? Were they close or a long way away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: I couldn't really tell how close they were. I don't even know how far away they were. Perhaps it's two or three metres away, depending on who was where. I couldn't really see it very well, you know, because we were all so upset. We were trying to save our lives, and I couldn't really see how far away people were. There was shooting going on, there was a fire all over the place, and, of course, a person has to be frightened under such circumstances. You know, it is so tragic, so you can't really notice all these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you see soldiers in any other place near the Sutre shop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: I did not see any other soldiers. I saw some in passing as I was getting there but not at that point in time because I was between two hills, so I couldn't see from there. I could only see this open area from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Could you recognise which military group these soldiers belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: I could recognise them because they passed by my house; the same uniformed soldiers with HVO insignia and with white ribbons on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what happened to Nadira? You said she was shot. Can you tell the Court what happened to her. Did she live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Nadira was sitting in front of me. She was hit in the head. At that moment, she didn't say anything. She lay on the right-hand side. She put her hands together on the right-hand side. She was there near me. My family members visited her -- she was taken to the hospital. However, she died eventually. She did not survive this because this bullet had hit her in the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did Hajra also die?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Hajra also died. She was hit in the chest and she died immediately. She died right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How far away from you was she when she was hit in the chest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Hajra was two or three metres away from me because we were all together in a group. I was going back and passing by her, and I heard what she said. "I was hit," she said. It was, I don't know, two or three metres, but I heard her say, "I was hit." (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: (redacted) I don't know how long they stayed, I don't know who gave them first aid, I don't know whether they went some place because I went back and they stayed by their sister who was killed, that is the mother, this other sister, and this wounded sister, and (redacted) too. They all stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that you decided to go back to your house where you were staying.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: (redacted) She left her son and husband behind, (redacted)and she said that we should hide that we would not survive either because they killed both her son and her husband. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: redacted) and she heard people crying and moaning and she joined them there and stayed there, and she went to Travnik (redacted), and I, my brother, and my son stayed at this house in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: This(redacted) lived in Ahmici, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: (redacted)came to Ahmici as a refugee, but she lived with her husband in(redacted), so she was a refugee in Ahmici. She settled down there, and I think that that was her sister's house. She had an apartment in Vitez. So they gave her the house, they let her stay there so that she could have shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court why it was that you decided to go back to your house and not continue on to Upper Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: My decision was made. I was wounded. If I went further ahead, there would be more woundings, the shooting wouldn't stop, so I tried to get out some other way. When I came back, the shooting still went on, so I was really forced to go back to the house. I didn't know where to go. I was unfamiliar with the surroundings. I didn't know the terrain. I didn't know which way I could pass and which way I could not pass. So the only thing I could decide was to go back to the house. You know, it was a question of life or death. I didn't know whether another bullet would hit me eventually, so I really had no other choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After receiving the advice from (redacted), you stated that you hid in the pit in a garage. Is that garage next to the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You stated a short while later, some soldiers came to the house and took your family away; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes, that is also correct. The garage that I hid in was next to the house. It was a biggish garage, there were two or three doors there, and I was at one of these entrances. This is where I hid because I knew that there was a kind of shelter there. I knew that there was a pit there. That is where the person who had lived in that house kept his fruit and vegetables during the winter, so I decided to stay underground because that is sometimes the best thing to do and, in other situations, it's the worst thing to do. It is true that two soldiers came and that they took my family away, and from this house of mine, they took out all electrical appliances, a video recorder, TV set, a mini stereo line that was there, and they took it out of the house and they torched the house and it burned down. Only ashes were left. I saw them leave too. I saw them when they came. I saw the house on fire. The garage which was next to the house was not on fire yet, so we stayed in this shelter. In the morning, I don't know what time it was, it seemed to me that a lot of time had gone by, but perhaps it was very early in the morning, two soldiers came. They took these things and put them into a red car. They drove it away. They didn't touch anything else. A short while after they left, four armed soldiers came to this house. They walked up to the house which had burned down. They walked into the garage. One of them wore civilian clothes. He had a blue track suit on and he wore his cap backwards. He was armed, he had a gun and a knife. They were talking and they were wondering what to do with the rest. They said, "Why not burn this down too? If nothing else is left, why should this remain?"

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: (redacted) and they were saying, "Torch this. This is paper and wooden board. It would burn better." I heard all of that. I heard it. I couldn't see them, though, because this soldier was standing above my head and it was only the trap door to this pit that was between us and it was covered with a wooden board and paper. And he said, "Burn it." So the remaining part of the garage, where I was still in this pit -- I don't know. I had to make a decision. There were only two ways out: either to burn alive or to get out and get shot by a bullet. I got out of this pit. I went into one of the corners of the garage. As the soldiers were shooting and catching chickens, we jumped out of the garage, went by the burnt house, and stayed there for about four or five days underneath a staircase because that is the only thing that hadn't burned down because it was made of concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I could stop you there, Witness, just so that the Court is clear about when things occurred? You went into the pit on the 16th of April; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The soldiers, two soldiers, came to your house, or to the house opposite the pit, and took your family away a few hours after going into the pit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What military group were those soldiers from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: The soldiers belonged to the HVO group. They had HVO insignia, they also had HVO patches, two soldiers in camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After your family was taken away, about how long after did other soldiers or soldiers come to the house and take the electrical equipment away or take it out of the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: After a short while -- I mean, I can't really tell you because this was a very short period of time, half an hour, an hour, the soldiers came back and took the things away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, were they the same two soldiers that arrested your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: I think that they were the same two soldiers who had arrested my family because I was watching all of this through a small hole where a small window was, so I cannot really say for sure. It was a very small window, 20 by 20, but I think those were the same two soldiers, those who had taken out these things from the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: They had taken the things out of the house, and where did they put them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: They put them into this garage next to me, which was the garage next to the house, and at that point, the house was torched and it burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was it those same two soldiers that set a light to the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who set a light to the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Those were the same two soldiers. I mean, yes, that is true, those who took away the things and those who set the house on fire, because they took the things out and they set the house on fire on the 16th of April and the things remained in the garage until the 17th of April. The two soldiers who took these things out of the house burned the house the same day, (redacted)house, I mean, and other soldiers put the garage on fire the next day. Those were not the same soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The following day, did someone come and pick up the electrical equipment, on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes, yes. These two same soldiers who collected the things, the other things, they came the next day and they took these things away in a red car. I don't know what make it was. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then you mentioned that the place that you were in was set alight sometime later that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Correct. I mean, the next day, because I spent the night there in this shelter, I spent the night in this shelter. And the next day, after these soldiers left, those who had taken the things away, two other soldiers came after a certain period of time or, rather, four soldiers came after a certain period of time. They walked up to the garage, they tried to find certain things and, as I said, they came, they searched the place. The garage was locked. They broke the door down. I saw all of that. And then these other four soldiers torched the garage that I was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to say which military group these soldiers that torched the garage, who they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Those soldiers belonged to the HVO group. They wore HVO patches and I saw HVO insignia, and that is probably the formations that they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then you said you hid in the house for four or five days, I think.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, I hid in the burned house. When the garage was torched, I had to leave it. Otherwise, I would have burned alive because the garage had burned down too. So then we ran to the other house, the burnt house. In that house, everything had burned down except for this part --

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can show you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: -- that was going upstairs. I mean, I'm talking about the concrete staircase, so we could hide for four or five days underneath the concrete staircase.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask that the witness be shown a map of the house and the shed -- or the sheds in which he stayed in whilst these activities were occurring.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The map is marked 213.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, looking at the map that's in front of you, does that resemble the house and the shed or larger garage area in which you stayed on the 16th and 17th and then for that four and five days after the 16th and 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes. This is the house. It was a four-roofed house. This is a shed, this is a house. This is the house that burned down, the family house that burned down, the family of(redacted). This is the entrance into this house, from this side. All of this was the kitchen. In this corner was the garage -- the pantry, sorry. That is where they put their things away. Here was one garage, here was another garage, and then a third one and a fourth one. All of this was underneath a single roof, but there were different doors. And this is where I was (indicating). Here, underneath the threshold, that is where the pit I was telling you about is, and there is a small window there, a very small window through which I managed to see what was going on between this house and this garage. So this is the house, this is where the gate is, so then you walk in through the gate and then you can either walk into the house or go further on to this garage where I had survived, where I was, and then over here is the staircase where we took shelter afterwards, and you take those stairs when you're going upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you mark with a red marker with an X the place where the pit was where you stayed on the 16th and 17th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes, yes, fine. (Marks). This is it. Here, this is the entrance and this is where the pit was and here, underneath the threshold, was a small window which was there really for ventilation. So this is where the pit was. It was about one metre, one and a half metres below.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. After you left the pit and went to the house, you said you stayed there for about four or five days and you were with your son and your brother; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court or explain to the Court how you survived for those four or five days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Those four or five days, life was quite difficult, hard. The shooting was still on. I didn't know who was where, where the rest of my family members were. The first two days, we were hungry, and we tried to find something to eat there. We had water. We had no fire. Underneath that staircase, we found some sugar and there was some apple juice too. We took it, we drank this apple juice and we ate sugar, and that is how we lived in this particular shelter over those four or five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, the answer may be obvious to you, but can you explain to the Court why you didn't leave that house for that period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: I did not leave the house during that time because I didn't know which way to go, how to get out, how to save my life. The shooting was still on. There was unrest, something strange was going on. I was sitting there, standing there waiting and hoping that someone would come from humanitarian organisations to help these people, to make peace. One day, we heard the sound of tanks. When UNPROFOR came with their soldiers, they were collecting corpses. They were looking for people who were dead and alive. I saw through a small window which was in this shelter where we were, from Gornji Ahmici, from the upper mosque, that is, I saw two tanks pass by and I saw them go in the direction of Vitez. After a short while, when they went to Vitez, four men came up -- I don't know if they were soldiers. They weren't armed. They wore blue uniforms and they had air masks on their faces and they were looking to see what was in this burnt house. I thought that they were soldiers of UNPROFOR and I revealed myself to them. I walked out of the shelter. I surrendered. I didn't know who they were. One of these soldiers wore a first aid sign. He asked, "Are you alive?" And I said, "Yes." He said, "Get out." And I got out. "Are you wounded?" "Yes, I am. These two aren't." I cannot say who this soldier was because they were just saying, "Hey! Take these four guys." This soldier walked up and I saw him wearing HVO insignia, and they took us away into a house at the collection centre. They brought us there. So that is where we were. We came to a house, one after the other. It was -- I don't know whose house it was, a low house with a balcony. I know that we went by the soccer fields, but I don't know whose house this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness U, if you would stop there for a moment? The four men who came in the blue uniforms with the gas masks, did they seem to be associated with the soldier you referred to as an HVO soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: These four men, when they came, these four lads, these four soldiers, they were wearing blue uniforms, Civil Defence uniforms, and one of them had the first aid emblem. They were not armed. The fifth soldier, who was wearing a camouflage uniform with an HVO insignia, that one was armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And they were together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes, and they were together. These four lads were under the escort, they were escorted by this armed soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did anyone in that group tell you they were picking up dead bodies, or did you assume that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Nobody told me that they were collecting corpses, but as I was getting out to the gate, through the gate of(redacted) house, I saw a dead body by the gate post, and that is why I assumed that they were collecting dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who was that person? Who was that dead body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: In my opinion, as far as I could see, (redacted). He could have been that. You could recognise his face but only ever so slightly because the face had already been partly destroyed, but it seemed to me that indeed it was (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you say whether or not that body was there previous to these four masked men and this soldier arriving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: I didn't walk around. I didn't see it before I came out and saw those four soldiers. I didn't see that. I hadn't seen that dead body. It was at that very moment when these four soldiers arrived, that is when I saw the dead body lying by the gate through which we had come out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just to clear something up, the masks, they were gas masks as opposed to disguises?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes, they were gas masks, protective masks, protective masks which served to keep out poisons and things like that. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have about probably 15 more minutes with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thirty-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: By the way, before you start, I wonder whether you will provide -- you will hand over to us the list of witnesses for the next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Maybe by lunch time?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: We do have it with us now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I've just been told by lunch time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We're planning to go on until half past twelve, then have a one-hour break for lunch, and then to resume at half past one until three.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I just have a few more questions in open session, and then I would ask it to be closed to clear up a few details. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning again.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: We left off a moment ago when you told us that after you stayed in the house for about five or six days -- or about four or five days, sorry, you were taken by a HVO soldier to a collection point, a house. Can you tell the Court basically where that collection point was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: That collection point, that house, was in the area of Zume by the soccer playground, by the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I actually didn't have the channel earpiece on. I just wonder if that last answer could be repeated by the translator.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That collection point, that house, was in the area of Zume by the soccer playground, by the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That house, was it in the Croat area of Zume or the Muslim area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: That was in the Croatian section of Zume.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How did you get there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: When we left this house, the soldier who was escorting the patrol had us file in a column one after another, and thus we were escorted by the soldier and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you see any damaged houses on the way to the collection area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: In the area where the Muslim population was most of the houses were damaged, burnt down, and in the section where the Croatian population was, not a single house was damaged at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who was in charge of the collection area, which military group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: The military group in charge was the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what type of people were collected there, what ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: There were the Croatian people, the Bosnian-Croatian people, who were there where the collection centre was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How many Muslims were at the collection area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: I do not know. In that part of Zume only three of us arrived, and I did not know the others. Or perhaps they were hidden in shelters elsewhere, but it was the three of us that had arrived. There were no others then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how many HVO soldiers were at the collection area, at the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: A number of soldiers, about ten of them, were there, but not only soldiers were there, there were also civilians sitting in front of the house. We were there, we did not go into the house. We gave our particulars, who we are, what we did, and it was all, again -- and again under the control of the HVO. We had to go on to the camp, to the so-called camp of Dubravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Other than yourselves, the three of you, yourself, your brother, your son, were any other people taken to that house in that arrested situation like yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: I don't know about that particular time -- I know about that particular time, I don't know about before it, because as I told you, I came to that house, that collection centre, after three or four days, I'm not quite sure. And whether anybody had been there or taken to it prior to our arrival, I really don't know. When we came, at that moment there was no one else of the people that I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you were taken to the Dubravica school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Yes, to the Dubravica camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who was in charge of that camp, which military group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Here, again, it was the HVO that was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how many civilians were at that camp, other than yourselves, your brother, and your son and yourself, or other people perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: As for the exact number I can't say, because there was a large number of civilians in that camp, quite a few people in a hall in which we were. There were between 150 and 200 people, sometimes more and sometimes less, but that was not the only place where people were accommodated. And how many people were in the other section side, I didn't go there, I didn't see. But in this particular room there were between 150 and 200 women, children and men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And from your time there, are you able to say which ethnic group they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: The imprisoned people? Do you mean the people who were in the camp, to which is the group they belonged?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: The people there were all Bosnian Muslims, belonged to the ethnic group of Bosnian Muslims, all of those who were prisoners there then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were you spoken to by anyone in charge of the camp, or anyone associated with the control of the camp? Were you interrogated there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: As soon as we got there there was a room, an office, where we gave our names, when we came, when we left, how we reached Ahmici, where we were, what we were, what our intentions were. There were three soldiers there. They wore HVO insignia. We had to give all necessary information about our movements, et cetera. Then we were taken into a larger room. I told you that 150 or 200 women, and children and men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you stayed at that camp for what period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: I didn't stay there long. I stayed four to five days -- six days, rather, to the best of my recollection. Then the organisation for first-aid came, the UNHCR, and they said that I was wounded, they made sure, and I was taken to the hospital in Zenica. And my brother and son stayed on for some 20 odd days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell the court where these people had come from? These 150 to 200 civilians, what areas of Vitez did they come from, or the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: We talked. There were refugees who were in Donja Dubravica, who were around the railway station, around the road and these less populated areas too. There were also women and children from Ahmici who managed to get out. There were women and men who were from the so-called railway station. This is an area of Donji Vitez. You know, from all these parts there were women, and children and men, but mostly there were men from Donji Vitez, and there were less women.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were people free to leave that school of their own volition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After leaving the Dubravica school, did you go to hospital in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: Then I went to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you had an operation there and you stayed in the hospital for four months?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: They operated on me there, and then after -- actually, I had to stay in hospital for some time, and then only they found the time to operate me, and then I stayed on in the hospital. Altogether it was less than four months.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain to the Court the injury you received from being shot and the effect that it's had on your arm since then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: At first it was a very small wound, but I remained disabled as far as my left arm is concerned. My nerve was broken, so I cannot control practically all of my left arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Is that still the case today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: That is still the case today. In addition to certain attempts to operate, the situation has, nevertheless, remained the same, and that arm remains disabled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you left the village of Ahmici and were taken to -- and was taken to the collection centre in Zume, can you tell the Court whether there appeared to be any other Muslim civilians still living in that part of the village that you walked through?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U.
utterances.text: I didn't see a single one. I believe -- I think that all the Muslims from -- expelled from Ahmici and from Zume -- have been expelled from Ahmici and Zume. There I found some people who had lived in Zume, but they had been banished, so that I believe that not a single Muslim soul had remained in Zume.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I would ask that the Court go into closed session now. I have just a few photographs and a just a couple of names to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. All right. We'll move into closed session. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: redacted redacted redacted (The witness entered court) (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Will you please read the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness V. I am going to hand, at this time, to the usher a slip of paper with the name of this witness on it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked 217.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think we can perhaps begin in open session, and as we get into some more details, we may have to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Witness V, you have asked for some protection measures, that is that your name and face be protected, and those measures have been granted by the Tribunal, so you can feel confident in providing full and complete testimony here today. If there comes a time during the course of your testimony that we need to ask you questions about information that might disclose your identity, we will at that point ask the Tribunal to go into closed session, and what that means is that your voice will not leave this room and no one outside this room will hear what you're saying, and during those occasions when that becomes necessary, you can feel confident in providing full and complete information and testimony about those matters. Do you understand what I've just said and do you have any questions about what I've just said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V.
utterances.text: Yes. I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: We will be referring to you from time to time as Witness V. Now, to begin, Witness V, could you tell us, prior to April of 1993, where did you live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V.
utterances.text: I lived in Ahmici in my own home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you and do you have a family, and without naming their names, tell us the composition of your family back in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V.
utterances.text: I have a wife and two sons, and during the conflict, I had only one son, as far as my nuclear family is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us in what year you were born or how old you are?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V.
utterances.text: Thirty-one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned the conflict, and the conflict that I will be referring to at this time is the conflict in April of 1993. Do you remember that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I want to focus your attention just briefly now on the day before the day of the conflict. Do you remember seeing anything during the course of that day, the day before, that aroused some suspicion in your mind about what might happen the next day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V.
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was a bit suspicious. I came into the village because I was going to visit my mother-in-law, and as I was going back by car and I passed a curve by Vlatko Kupreskic's, I saw from the car a group of soldiers, perhaps ten of them altogether, and two civilians in front of the house of Zoran Kupreskic, on the cross-roads between Zoran's and Ivica's place. That's where it was. I saw that some people had gathered there and that something was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How did you know they were soldiers, these people in front of Zoran Kupreskic's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V.
utterances.text: Well, they wore camouflage uniforms and they had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what time of day this was that you saw those soldiers in that -- near that house, the Zoran Kupreskic house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V.
utterances.text: It was the afternoon, perhaps about 5.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned Zoran Kupreskic. Prior to the attack in '93, in the days or perhaps weeks prior to that attack, did you have occasion to see Zoran Kupreskic in or around Ahmici in a uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V.
utterances.text: Yes, yes. On one occasion, as I was passing by in my car, I left my home and I was going towards Vitez, and as I passed by the mosque in my car, I saw him and his neighbour Dragan Vidovic. They both wore uniforms and they both had weapons, and they were going towards their house -- I mean, in the direction of their houses. This was just when the conflict was. I don't know, either that day or the next day when the fighting was going on in the village of Kovacevac, when Kovacevac had fallen, when it was taken by the Croats. That's when it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Was this before the attack on Ahmici in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: By the way, when you saw Zoran Kupreskic and his neighbour Dragan Vidovic in uniform with weapons, were these two men on foot or were they in an automobile?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V.
utterances.text: They were on foot and I was in a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you know Dragan Papic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: In the days and weeks before the attack on Ahmici, did you ever see him in a uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V.
utterances.text: Yes, I did, many times. In Ahmici, by his house, or in town, in Vitez, I saw him in a black uniform which he usually wore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, after having observed the day before the attack these soldiers, did you notify anyone, tell anyone, and if so, who and then was there any decision taken about what you had seen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V.
utterances.text: After I had seen this, I talked to some neighbours of mine, and I told them about this gathering, and some other people had seen it too, and a decision was made to reinforce these controls -- these patrols, these guards, so that we could see what these soldiers in front of the house would do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you go on patrol that night, the night before the attack or the early morning of the attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V.
utterances.text: Well, yes, yes. I went. I was there from 2.00 until 4.00. I even stayed until 4.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, at this time, I'm going to ask the witness to look at a map which may require us -- I think will require us, with the permission of the Court, to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Witness V, for the next several questions, we're still in open session, just to let you know. If you could, with the pointer that you have in your hand now, could you show us the house of Zoran Kupreskic where you saw those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V.
utterances.text: I saw it over here, here, this cross-roads, here between Ivica's house and Zoran's house, over here (indicating). Yeah, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, do you see the two houses across the road from Ivica's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were the soldiers in between those two houses or were they in front of one house or the other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V.
utterances.text: In front of these two houses. That's where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness had already answered exactly, before that, the position of the house and of the soldiers, and he said they were between Zoran's and Ivica's house. Now when the question is being put time and again by the Prosecutor, now the Prosecutor is trying to place these soldiers in front of my client's house, and I think that that is wrong and I object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness said very accurately that he saw these soldiers at the cross-roads, so he already positioned them and said exactly where they were. So the rest, I believe, is mere repetition of a question that has already been answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I agree. Could you move on to another question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you please place a mark where you remember seeing those soldiers, using that crayon or that marker in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V.
utterances.text: (Marks). In this area here, so it's this house and that house, in this direction, this way, on the road. That is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Just for the record, you've placed a line along that road that goes between those three houses, Ivica, Zoran, and Mirjan Kupreskic's house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you also indicated that you had seen Zoran Kupreskic in a uniform with his friend Dragan Vidovic some time earlier. Could you turn around for us and look at that big blow-up behind you, using your pointer, could you show us where you recall seeing Zoran and Dragan Vidovic that day? If you could turn the other way, I think it's probably easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but he did not say that -- I mean, the witness did not say what the Prosecutor is saying now, that on that day, he saw Zoran and Vidovic on the road. The witness said that he saw Zoran and Vidovic on the road, but before that, before that day, so not on that day, not on the 15th, but when Kovacevac had fallen. I think this is a different time completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I think there is a translation problem or a miscommunication. I did not mean the same day he saw the soldiers in front of the house of Zoran and -- he, I think, clearly said it was an earlier time period during the fall of Kovacevac, and that's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Witness V, that day, the day you saw Dragan and Zoran in uniform, could you point to the blow-up map and show us where they were when you saw them that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V.
utterances.text: I saw them exactly as Kovacevac had fallen. This is the village of Donja Rovna and the village of Kovacevac -- I don't know exactly where they are. On the day of that conflict or a day after that conflict, when fighting was on up there, I was passing by in my car in this part where the mosque was. I was passing by in my car, and they were going this way, this way (indicating), towards their house. That's where I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, there are two mosques in Ahmici. Which mosque are you referring to, just for purposes of the record? And perhaps you can refer to minaret, with and without, might be a good way of making a distinction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V.
utterances.text: That's the mosque with the minaret, which is in the lower part of the village, somewhere around here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: When you indicated with your pointer and said that they were going "this way," could you be more specific, just for the record? Which way were they going? In which direction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V.
utterances.text: Well, they were going in the direction of their houses, from that place. So from the direction of Kovacevac towards their houses, from the main road that leads to Vitez, and then when you turn off to Ahmici, they were going towards their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I think, at this time, we would request a closed session because we will ask for some identifying information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Can we go into a closed session? (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Whereupon proceedings adjourned at 3.35 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 28th day of September, 1998, at 8.30 a.m.
